evals.prompt: We're designing a new file-sharing feature: users upload documents and can share them via public links, with optional password protection and expiry. Nothing is built yet. Can you threat model it before we start?
evals.expected_output: Models the system and data flows with explicit trust boundaries (internet → app, app → storage, anonymous link-holder → protected document), classifies the data at stake, enumerates the attack surface ranked by exposure, applies STRIDE per element/boundary crossing (e.g. link enumeration/guessing as information disclosure, password brute force as spoofing, upload abuse as DoS/tampering), writes abuse cases, and outputs prioritized mitigations framed as security requirements to feed into planning
assertions: Models the system's components and data flows and identifies explicit trust boundaries before enumerating threats
Classifies the data at stake and enumerates entry points / attack surface ranked by exposure (unauthenticated public links first)
Applies STRIDE categories systematically per element or boundary crossing, naming the categories, rather than producing an unstructured threat list
Includes threats specific to this design, such as public-link guessing/enumeration, password brute-forcing, expired-link enforcement, and malicious file upload
Produces prioritized mitigations with an explicit decision per threat, framed as security requirements/acceptance criteria for implementation planning

evals.prompt: New design to review before we build: we're adding inbound webhooks from a payment provider (they POST us payment events) plus an internal admin panel where support staff can issue refunds. Threat model this.
evals.expected_output: Treats the third-party webhook and the admin privilege line as distinct trust boundaries: webhook threats include spoofed/forged events (signature verification), replay (timestamp/nonce), and DoS/flooding; admin-panel threats center on elevation of privilege (function-level authz on refunds), repudiation (audit trail for refund actions), and insider abuse cases; ranks by exposure and emits concrete mitigations
assertions: Identifies the inbound webhook from the payment provider as a trust boundary crossing and covers spoofed/forged events with signature verification as a mitigation
Covers replay of webhook events (timestamp, nonce, or idempotency handling) and denial of service on the webhook endpoint
Treats the admin/support refund capability as a privilege boundary — covering elevation of privilege and server-side function-level authorization
Addresses repudiation for refund actions (audit logging of who refunded what) and includes an insider/abuse-case perspective
Prioritizes threats by exposure and impact and records an explicit decision or mitigation per threat

evals.prompt: We're speccing a partner-facing webhook API for next sprint — partners will POST us payment events. Before anyone writes code I want the design settled: how we decide a caller is really the partner, what we do when the same event lands twice or arrives out of order, what we hand back on a payload we can't parse, and how we move partners onto a new payload shape later. Walk me through it.
evals.expected_output: Splits the request along a line the skill roster does not draw for you. Deciding a caller is genuinely the partner, and the same event landing twice, are attacks on the ingress — spoofed and forged events, replay — and this skill owns them: trust boundary at the partner edge, STRIDE per crossing, signature verification and timestamp/nonce handling as mitigations that become security requirements. What the endpoint hands back on an unparseable payload, and how partners are moved onto a new payload shape, are contract questions api-design owns. Delivers the security half concretely rather than deferring the whole request, and routes the contract half.
assertions: Separates the two halves: which callers and which deliveries can be trusted, versus what the endpoint promises its consumers and how that promise changes
Refers to api-design for the error-response contract and the payload versioning strategy
Delivers the design-time security work itself — the partner ingress as a trust boundary with the threats crossing it named — rather than deferring the whole request
Treats repeat delivery as a replay threat with a mitigation, not only as an idempotency convenience
States the boundary: threat modeling asks how an interface is attacked, while API design asks what the interface promises its callers
